paragraphs.source_en: The theory of an evolution from Kel Essuf engravings into the Round Head paintings which was proposed by Mori (1967), the Halliers (1999) and by Striedter, Tauveron and Ferhat (2002-3) is based on superimpositions and on the presumed evolution of figures, supposing a development of forms from simple towards more complex ones. Thus, the originally extremely simple Kel Essuf engravings would acquire more details such as fingers or other attributes. Later, only paintings were made, leading to the creation of evolved Round Head figures with more details than engravings. Such a hypothesis is possible but difficult to prove due to the lack of direct dating of the Kel Essuf engravings.

paragraphs.source_en: The difference in forms between various Kel Essuf engravings may also be explained as the intentional differentiation of groups or individuals who created them. Yet, although they differ slightly in form and attributes, the Kel Essuf present, as well as the Round Head paintings, a strong homogeneity in all regions where they are found.

paragraphs.source_en: Another fact supporting the relationship between the Kel Essuf and the Round Head images is their coexistence in the same area, namely the lower altitudes of the Acacus, Algerian Tadrart and Djado, which is also the area of the presumed earliest Round Heads. Whilst Muzzolini (1995a) claims that Round Head art is exclusively painted, the Halliers (1999) believe that they consist of both paintings and engravings. The second hypothesis is plausible since the engravings are often present in the shelters, unlike the Bubaline engravings which are always located in the open. The coexistence of the Kel Essuf and Round Heads on the same walls indicates that the same places were considered important for imagemaking, which may have been separated in time but may have also been (at least partially) contemporaneous.
